findings.title: Device is cached before DB write, so a rejected device is let through on retry
findings.body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device key into localCache (line 87) and only afterwards calls anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice (line 93). When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which is now propagated (line 147) and by client.go aborts authentication. However the cache entry is never removed on this failure. Any subsequent request from the same device within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the early `localCache.Get` return (line 83) and succeeds without touching the DB. The net effect is that the device limit only blocks the first request of a device (per instance) and then silently allows it, the device is never recorded in the DB/count, and because the cache is per-process the behavior also differs across HA instances. The cache must be populated only after a successful DB write (or deleted on error).

findings.title: Count-then-insert check is not atomic, so the device limit can be exceeded
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice reads CountDevices (line 110) and then, if under the limit, performs a separate INSERT/ON CONFLICT (line 149) in a different DB session with no transaction or lock between them. Under concurrent anonymous requests two or more new devices can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, pushing the table past the configured limit. The limit is therefore only approximately enforced under load. Consider counting and inserting in one transaction/locking, or enforcing the cap in SQL.

findings.title: Returning the raw limit error from Authenticate fails anonymous requests instead of denying gracefully
findings.body: When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns `nil, err`. Because this is the anonymous authn client, a returned error aborts authentication for the whole request rather than yielding a successful anonymous identity, so a device that is over the limit gets an authentication failure (generic error/401-500) on the requests where the DB path runs. Combined with the localCache being primed before the DB call, this produces intermittent failures: the first request fails and later ones (cache hit) succeed. There is no user-facing handling for 'device limit reached'; the decision to hard-fail the request (vs. logging and continuing, or mapping to a controlled response) should be made explicit.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit typed as number | undefined but backend always sends a number
findings.body: FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit is an int64 without omitempty, so the API always serializes a number (0 when unset / unlimited). The TS type `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined` and the GrafanaBootConfig default `undefined` therefore misrepresent the wire contract: consumers checking for `undefined` to mean 'unset' will never see it, they always get 0. The type should be `number` (with 0 documented as unlimited) to match the backend.

findings.title: Limit test only covers rejection of a new device; no coverage that existing devices still update
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit verifies only that a brand-new device is rejected when the limit is reached. It does not assert the complementary and important behavior that an already-registered, active device continues to update successfully at the limit (the updateDevice path returning rowsAffected > 0), nor does it cover the localCache-before-DB-write interaction that lets a rejected device through on retry. Without these cases the bypass and the 'existing devices keep working' contract are untested.
